topic.focus: How a small Danish island became energy self-sufficient

candidate_instructions: Read all five sections. Answer Questions 1-10. Follow the stated word limits exactly.

sections.heading: A community experiment
sections.text: In 1997, the Danish island of Samsø won a government competition to become the country's first renewable energy community. At the time, the island's four thousand residents imported almost all of their electricity and heating oil from the mainland. Few people believed that farmers and fishermen could transform their energy supply within a decade. Yet the project's leader, an engineer named Søren Hermansen, insisted that the change had to come from the islanders themselves rather than from outside investors.

sections.heading: Turning wind into ownership
sections.text: The first step was wind power. Eleven large turbines were built on land between 1998 and 2002, and crucially, many turbines are owned collectively by residents who bought shares in them. A single share cost roughly the price of a used car, and more than four hundred and fifty islanders became co-owners. Because the profits stayed on the island, even people who had opposed the turbines at first began to see them as a shared investment rather than an intrusion on the landscape.

sections.heading: Resistance and persuasion
sections.text: Not everyone welcomed the plans. Several farmers initially refused to allow cables to cross their fields, and some residents worried that the turbines would spoil the island's quiet character and harm tourism. Hermansen spent years attending village meetings, drinking coffee in farmhouse kitchens, and adjusting the plans. In one case, a turbine site was moved half a kilometre simply to keep the peace between two neighbouring families.

sections.heading: Heat from straw and sun
sections.text: Electricity was only part of the answer. The island also built district heating plants that burn local straw, a waste product from the farms, to warm most of the houses in the main villages. Solar panels cover the roof of one plant, and surplus heat is stored in large water tanks for cloudy days. Farmers who once burned their straw in the fields now sell it, which gives them a new source of income.

sections.heading: An exportable idea
sections.text: By 2007, Samsø produced more renewable electricity than it consumed, and today the island exports its surplus electricity to the Danish mainland through an undersea cable. Visitors arrive from Japan, the United States, and across Europe to study the model. Hermansen's energy academy now teaches other communities that the technology matters less than the trust between neighbours, because, as he often says, machines do not vote at village meetings.

passage.full_text:
Paragraph 1 — A community experiment
In 1997, the Danish island of Samsø won a government competition to become the country's first renewable energy community. At the time, the island's four thousand residents imported almost all of their electricity and heating oil from the mainland. Few people believed that farmers and fishermen could transform their energy supply within a decade. Yet the project's leader, an engineer named Søren Hermansen, insisted that the change had to come from the islanders themselves rather than from outside investors.

Paragraph 2 — Turning wind into ownership
The first step was wind power. Eleven large turbines were built on land between 1998 and 2002, and crucially, many turbines are owned collectively by residents who bought shares in them. A single share cost roughly the price of a used car, and more than four hundred and fifty islanders became co-owners. Because the profits stayed on the island, even people who had opposed the turbines at first began to see them as a shared investment rather than an intrusion on the landscape.

Paragraph 3 — Resistance and persuasion
Not everyone welcomed the plans. Several farmers initially refused to allow cables to cross their fields, and some residents worried that the turbines would spoil the island's quiet character and harm tourism. Hermansen spent years attending village meetings, drinking coffee in farmhouse kitchens, and adjusting the plans. In one case, a turbine site was moved half a kilometre simply to keep the peace between two neighbouring families.

Paragraph 4 — Heat from straw and sun
Electricity was only part of the answer. The island also built district heating plants that burn local straw, a waste product from the farms, to warm most of the houses in the main villages. Solar panels cover the roof of one plant, and surplus heat is stored in large water tanks for cloudy days. Farmers who once burned their straw in the fields now sell it, which gives them a new source of income.

Paragraph 5 — An exportable idea
By 2007, Samsø produced more renewable electricity than it consumed, and today the island exports its surplus electricity to the Danish mainland through an undersea cable. Visitors arrive from Japan, the United States, and across Europe to study the model. Hermansen's energy academy now teaches other communities that the technology matters less than the trust between neighbours, because, as he often says, machines do not vote at village meetings.
